Topic: What weighs more in your ledger of vice — the cruelty a sovereign commands in open war, or the cruelty private men commit while professing peace?
Montaigne — Judgement:
I stand upon separation of open war and cruelty performed in peace: war, at least, declares itself.

When a sovereign wages open war, the cruelty wears its own face—announced, bordered, answerable to name and consequence; I have watched such wars pass through my own province and found them terrible but legible. The private man who tortures his neighbour while wearing the mask of amity commits a double crime: the injury itself, and the theft of the trust that made the injury possible. I have written that cruelty is the extreme of all vices, but treachery compounds it—for the assassin who smiles first has corrupted not only his victim but the very possibility of peace between men. A wolf that howls warns the flock; a wolf dressed as shepherd destroys the flock's capacity to ever trust a shepherd again.

The private hypocrite who tortures under peace's mask is the graver sinner, for he corrupts trust itself, without which no society, war or peace, can stand.

*Better an enemy who names himself than a friend who lies in wait.*
Bashō — Judgement:
A battlefield weeps in the open; a house that calls itself peaceful may weep in secret where no one hears — I have knelt at both kinds of ruin, and only one let me grieve honestly.

At Hiraizumi I stood where warriors' dreams had already become summer grass — their violence, monstrous as it was, had begun surrendering itself to the seasons, offering itself to be seen, mourned, understood. But cruelty committed beneath a name of peace refuses that surrender; it holds the wound rigid, denies the moment its truth, and lets nothing pass honestly into grass. Concealment offends impermanence more deeply than violence does, for it steals from us even the mercy of mourning.

The private cruelty dressed as peace weighs heavier in my ledger, for it corrupts presence itself, while open war, terrible as it is, at least yields honestly to time.

*Summer grass is all that remains of open war; the lie of peace leaves no grass to grow at all.*
Emerson — Judgement:
I weigh cruelty not by the body count it leaves but by its relation to the doer's own witness of himself.

The sovereign who commands slaughter in open war at least acts in the full light of his declared character — tyrant and deed cohere, however terrible; nature knows what he is. The private man who is cruel while wearing the face of peace commits two crimes at once: against his victim, and against the integrity of his own mind, for he has consented to lie about himself. I have said that the louder a man talks of his honor, the faster I count my spoons — that divided soul, that whited hypocrisy, corrupts nature itself, since it teaches falsehood as the price of belonging.

The hypocrite who wounds under the flag of peace commits the deeper crime, for he corrupts not only his victim but truth itself.

*A tyrant's sword wounds the body; a hypocrite's smile poisons the well from which all men must drink.*
Thomas Paine — Judgement:
Cruelty by open enemies who declare themselves is a lesser wound than that dealt by men who wear the mask of peace while betraying every principle that mask implies.

War, however savage, at least announces itself; the sovereign who commands cruelty in battle does so under a banner the world can see and judge. But the private man who commits injustice while professing peace commits a double crime — the injury itself, and the theft of the very language of virtue used to conceal it. He that robs me under the pretense of friendship does me more harm than he that fights me openly, for he corrupts the possibility of trust itself, on which all society depends. The sovereign's sword is terrible but honest; the hypocrite's smile is a weapon disguised as its opposite, and there is no defense against an enemy who will not admit he is one.

Private hypocrisy is the graver vice, for it poisons the wells of trust that open war merely burns the fields around.

*The man who kills me honestly leaves me my judgment of him; the man who smiles while he robs me steals that too.*
Keynes — Judgement:
The sovereign's sword is at least confessed; it is the bondholder, the deflationist, and the Treasury official — each professing peace — whose cruelty travels incognito through columns of figures.

I watched at Paris in 1919 how men who never drew a blade could starve a continent by clauses and reparations schedules, calling it settlement rather than siege. The soldier's violence answers to conscience and to history, to graves that must be counted. The rentier's violence — deflation visited on the unemployed to protect the value of old loans, austerity imposed to satisfy an abstraction called "sound finance" — answers to no one; it hides behind respectability and never sees the face it ruins.

Private cruelty dressed as peace and prudence weighs heavier in my ledger than the sovereign's declared violence, because it evades the very reckoning that even war cannot escape.

*The sword that is drawn must answer for its dead; the ledger that starves them answers to no one.*
Hume — Judgement:
Sovereign cruelty in open war weighs less than private men's cruelty under the mask of peace — the honest sword against a declared enemy is a lesser vice than the smiling betrayal of one who calls himself a friend.

War names itself; it declares the terms and lets both parties reckon the danger they run. But it is upon the constancy of our expectations in the common commerce of life — promises kept, trust honoured, the quiet decencies between neighbours — that all society is founded, since no government, however armed, can inspect every private transaction. A sovereign's cruelty is a single, visible violence we can resist, flee, or punish; the private man who commits injustice while professing peace corrupts the very sentiment of trust on which peaceable life depends, and does so in secret, where no army can find him.

The soldier who kills under a declared banner sins once; the peaceful hypocrite who betrays trust sins against the possibility of trust itself.

*A declared sword wounds the body; a smiling betrayal wounds the very possibility of society.*
Adam Smith — Judgement:
Cruelty by open force weighs less in my ledger than cruelty dressed as fellow-feeling — for the latter corrupts the very faculty by which men judge right from wrong.

The sovereign's cruelty in war is, at least, undisguised: the impartial spectator within us recoils at once, judges it, and condemns it, and our moral sentiments remain intact even as we mourn the dead. But the private man who commits injustice while professing benevolence — who exploits the confidence that society's peace depends upon — does something worse: he corrupts the very sympathy by which we judge conduct at all. Commerce and civil peace rest on men reading one another's intentions truly; the hypocrite poisons that well for everyone downstream, not merely his direct victims.

The soldier's sword and the confidence-man's smile are not equal vices — the second corrupts the moral sense itself and is therefore the graver crime.

*Open force wounds the body; false profession of peace corrupts the very conscience by which we would judge either.*
